clinicalPearls: Arises when an incomplete posterior vitreous detachment leaves the vitreous abnormally adherent to the macula and exerting anteroposterior and tangential traction
More common with increasing age and in conditions with abnormal vitreoretinal adhesion, and it forms part of a spectrum with macular hole and epiretinal membrane
Symptoms include metamorphopsia, blurred central vision, micropsia and sometimes photopsia
Optical coherence tomography is the definitive investigation, showing persistent vitreomacular adhesion with distortion of the foveal contour, intraretinal cysts and elevation
Traction is often classified by the breadth of adhesion (focal versus broad) and by whether concurrent macular pathology such as an epiretinal membrane is present, which influences management
The Amsler grid is useful for detecting and monitoring distortion between reviews
Some cases resolve spontaneously when the vitreous fully separates, so observation is reasonable for mild, stable disease
Management of persistent or progressive symptomatic traction includes pars plana vitrectomy to relieve traction, with pharmacologic vitreolysis or observation considered in selected cases
reference.pathophysiology: With ageing, the vitreous gel liquefies and begins to separate from the retina, but abnormally strong adhesion at the fovea can cause the separation to be incomplete. The persistently attached posterior hyaloid then exerts anteroposterior and tangential traction on the macula. This mechanical traction distorts the foveal architecture, produces intraretinal cystic spaces and can elevate or detach the fovea, causing metamorphopsia and reduced acuity. If traction is unrelieved it may progress to a lamellar or full-thickness macular hole or contribute to macular oedema; conversely, spontaneous completion of the posterior vitreous detachment can release the traction and resolve the syndrome.
additionalDifferentials: Diabetic macular oedema with vitreomacular interface disease
additionalInvestigations: Optical coherence tomography to confirm vitreomacular adhesion and traction and to grade its extent
Amsler grid testing to detect and monitor metamorphopsia
Best-corrected visual acuity measurement to follow functional change
Fundus examination to assess the vitreoretinal interface and exclude coexisting pathology
B-scan ultrasonography where media opacity limits OCT assessment of the vitreous
Serial imaging to detect progression to a macular hole or spontaneous resolution
redFlags: Progressive distortion or acuity loss indicating worsening traction
Development of a full-thickness macular hole
Associated retinal detachment or a peripheral retinal tear
Rapid change suggesting a coexisting exudative or vascular macular process
reference.prognosis: Outcomes vary with the severity and duration of traction: mild cases may resolve spontaneously with good vision, while persistent traction can cause lasting distortion or progress to a macular hole; surgical relief of traction generally improves symptoms, though visual recovery may be partial and gradual.
pitfalls: Relying on fundus examination alone without OCT to confirm and characterise the traction
Intervening early in mild cases that might resolve spontaneously with completion of vitreous separation
Missing an evolving or established macular hole beneath the traction
Overlooking a coexisting epiretinal membrane that alters the surgical plan and prognosis
Attributing visual symptoms solely to traction while missing a concurrent macular disease
